questions.question: Describe two benefits of working in the hospitality industry.
questions.model_answer: two single-line facts earn the two marks. Mark scheme: you learn the industry and improve your customer-service skills (1); you build confidence and skills in problem-handling and negotiation (1).

questions.question: Explain key characteristics of hospitality personnel.
questions.model_answer: name the characteristic, then add its "why". Mark scheme: patience under pressure (1), because a calm member of staff conveys calm to customers; the ability to multi-task and prioritise (1), so the most urgent guest need is handled first. Notice Q3 asks what the job gives YOU (benefits); Q4 asks what you must show (characteristics). Don't swap them.

questions.question: Which of these is a hospitality service, not a product?
questions.model_answer: Ask "can the customer hold it?" If no, it is a service. Answer: C.

questions.question: Name the three sectors of the hospitality industry and give one example of each.
questions.model_answer: One mark per sector, but only with a correct example attached. Model answer: Commercial, a hotel run for profit. Voluntary, a charity soup kitchen. Public, catering in a government hospital.

questions.question: A school canteen funded by the government belongs to which sector?
questions.model_answer: Follow the money. Government money means public sector, whoever eats there. Answer: C. (A charity canteen funded by donations would be voluntary; that is the distractor trap.)

questions.question: Explain two functions of the Institute of Hospitality.
questions.model_answer: This is a 2+2 question: name each function (1), explain what it means in practice (1). Model answer: The Institute monitors and maintains standards in the industry (1), which means it sets the quality of work members are expected to reach (1). It also reviews continuing professional development, CPD, for members (1), which means it checks that workers keep training and learning throughout their careers (1).

questions.question: An owner has bought into an existing business and its established business model. Which type of business is this?
questions.model_answer: "bought into an existing brand and system" is the franchise's exam fingerprint. Mark scheme answer: a franchise. Notice the MCQ pattern: a one-sentence vignette restating a syllabus point, then near-neighbour distractors from the same topic. Business types also carry half of

questions.question: In a franchise, the person who buys the right to use the brand is called the:
questions.model_answer: The franchisor owns the brand; the franchisee buys in. Answer: B.

questions.question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of operating as a sole trader.
questions.model_answer: This is a 2+2 question. One mark to state each point, one mark to explain it. Model answer: One advantage is that the owner keeps all the profit (1), because there are no partners to share earnings with, so success rewards the owner directly (1). One disadvantage is unlimited liability (1), meaning the owner is personally responsible for all business debts, so their own savings or home could be taken to pay them (1).

questions.question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of buying a franchise.
questions.model_answer: 2+2 again: state, then explain. Model answer: One advantage is trading under a known brand with a proven system (1), so customers trust the business from day one and the franchisor provides training and support (1). One disadvantage is the fees and royalties (1), because the franchisee must pay the franchisor a share of income and follow strict rules, leaving little freedom and less profit (1).

questions.question: What does GDP stand for?
questions.model_answer: mark scheme answer: gross domestic product. A whole mark for one memorised term. Watch for distractors like "general domestic product" or "gross national product"; read every option before answering.

questions.question: Define the term GDP (Gross Domestic Product).
questions.model_answer: Two ideas earn the two marks: "total value of goods and services produced by a country" (1) "in one year" (1). Learn definitions word-perfect; definition marks are the cheapest marks on the paper.

questions.question: Explain two ways the hospitality industry contributes to the GDP of the U.K.
questions.model_answer: 2+2: name each way (1), explain the mechanism (1). Model answer: Hospitality employs millions of workers (1); their wages are spent in the wider economy, adding further value (1). It also attracts tourism (1); visitors from abroad spend foreign money in U.K. hotels and restaurants, acting like an export (1).

questions.question: Which of these is an INTERNAL factor for a restaurant?
questions.model_answer: Apply the control test: which one can the restaurant itself decide? Answer: C. The other three happen to the business from outside.

questions.question: Explain one internal factor and one external factor that could reduce a hotel's contribution to GDP.
questions.model_answer: 2+2: name each factor and say it is internal or external (1), then explain how it cuts the hotel's sales or value (1). Model answer: An internal factor is poor service quality from untrained staff (1); bad reviews spread, guests stop booking, and the hotel sells fewer room- nights (1). An external factor is a recession (1); customers across the whole economy have less money, so they cut holidays and eat out less, and the hotel's revenue falls through no fault of its own (1).

questions.question: Which is an example of an internal customer in a hotel?
questions.model_answer: mark scheme answer: a commis chef. A colleague inside the business is internal.

questions.question: Which is an example of an external customer?
questions.model_answer: mark scheme answer: a taxi driver. Note LRN's line here: the taxi driver buying or collecting from the business counts as an external customer. Internal and external appear as MCQs from both directions, so learn examples of each.

questions.question: Outline the requirements of (a) an internal colleague and (b) a disabled customer.
questions.model_answer: one line each. Mark scheme: a colleague may need sales or invoice information, or an email confirming conference numbers (1); a disabled customer may need an accessible table near the washroom and help with ordering and meals (1).

questions.question: State two ways employees provide effective customer service.
questions.model_answer: mark scheme: a polite, respectful meet-and-greet (1); staying attentive to customer needs throughout service (1). Two bullets, no paragraph.

questions.question: Which is the best example of an internal customer of a hotel restaurant?
questions.model_answer: Internal = inside the business, relying on your work. Answer: B.

options.C: A food blogger reviewing the menu

questions.question: Describe two ways an employee should adapt their service for a customer with hearing difficulties.
questions.model_answer: 2+2: name the adaptation (1), describe how it helps (1). Model answer: Face the customer directly when speaking (1) so they can read your lips and expressions (1). Provide a written menu or pen and paper (1) so orders can be confirmed accurately without relying on speech (1).

questions.question: How many allergens are on the FSA's regulatory list that food businesses must know?
questions.model_answer: the mark scheme names the FSA list of 14 foodstuffs. Answer: C. Be ready to name two, such as gluten, shellfish or mustard.

questions.question: State two ways a hotel can support customers with mobility issues before they arrive at the building.
questions.model_answer: the trick word is "before". Physical answers like ramps earn nothing here. Model answer: Publish access information on the website and social media (1); provide a contact so support can be requested ahead of the visit (1).

questions.question: Describe two steps an employee should take when handling a customer complaint.
questions.model_answer: 2+2: the step (1), why it works (1). Model answer: Listen to the whole complaint without interrupting (1), because the customer needs to feel heard before any solution will satisfy them (1). Apologise sincerely and act quickly to fix the problem (1), then follow up to check the customer is happy, which can turn a complainer into a returning guest (1).

questions.question: State three methods a restaurant could use to collect customer feedback.
questions.model_answer: One mark each, no explanation needed for "state". Model answer: Comment cards on tables; an online review site such as Google; a follow-up email survey after the visit. (Mystery shopper, social media, suggestion box also earn marks.)

questions.question: Explain two ways employees can make sure customers receive a consistent standard of service.
questions.model_answer: 2+2: the method (1), how it produces consistency (1). Model answer: Follow the business's SOPs every shift (1), because written procedures mean every employee performs tasks the same correct way (1). Attend pre-service team briefings (1), so all staff know the day's menu, allergies and VIPs and give guests the same accurate information (1).

questions.question: A manager asks a stranger to visit her café, order like a normal customer, observe the service and report back. This feedback method is called a:
questions.model_answer: secret visitor who orders, observes and reports = mystery shopper. Answer: B. Its strength is honesty: staff don't know they're being assessed.

questions.question: Explain two reasons customer feedback is valuable to a hospitality business.
questions.model_answer: 2+2: the reason (1), the because (1). This question tests point 2, not point 1, so don't list channels. Model answer: Feedback shows the business exactly what to fix (1), because customers report weaknesses, like inconsistent dishes, that managers may never notice themselves (1). A complaint handled well can win the customer back (1), because guests trust a business they have watched listen, apologise and put things right (1).

questions.question: State two reasons for working well within a team.
questions.model_answer: mark scheme: it maximises the success of the team and the business (1); it creates a pleasant working environment for colleagues (1). Any two syllabus reasons earn the marks; keep them to one line each.

questions.question: Which is a direct business benefit of positive team relationships?
questions.model_answer: Three options are the opposite of benefits. Answer: C.

questions.question: Explain two reasons why working as a team is important in a busy restaurant.
questions.model_answer: 2+2: reason (1), explanation (1). Model answer: Staff can cover for each other during rushes or sickness (1), so service continues smoothly and customers are not kept waiting (1). Team communication catches mistakes early (1), meaning errors are corrected before they reach the customer and cause complaints (1).

questions.question: State two ways a manager can encourage positive working relationships within a team.
questions.model_answer: Two one-line actions from list 2, e.g. hold regular team briefings so everyone knows the plan (1); run a reward programme that recognises and praises good work (1). Mentoring new staff, mixing shifts, and social events all score too. Actions, not benefits.

questions.question: Define the term "team dynamics".
questions.model_answer: Definition marks want the syllabus wording: the way team members' personalities, roles and relationships (1) affect how the team behaves and performs (1). Both halves, or you drop a mark.

questions.question: Describe two ways negative working relationships can affect team morale.
questions.model_answer: 2+2: the effect (1), the description of its impact (1). Model answer: Gossip and cliques form (1), making excluded staff feel unwelcome so they stop contributing to the team (1). Stress and absence increase (1), as unhappy staff avoid work, leaving shifts short-handed and morale even lower (1).

questions.question: A waiter believes his manager is treating him unfairly and wants to raise a formal complaint. Which procedure should he use?
questions.model_answer: Grievance is raised BY the worker; disciplinary is action AGAINST a worker. He is raising a complaint, so answer: B.

questions.question: Which of the following is most likely to cause conflict in a hospitality team?
questions.model_answer: Three options are prevention measures. Answer: C.

questions.question: List three ways conflict can emerge within a hospitality team.
questions.model_answer: Three one-line causes, no explanation needed for "list". Any three of: poor communication or misunderstandings; unfair workloads or rotas; personality clashes; competition for tips, hours or promotion; stress during busy service; unclear job roles; cultural or language misunderstandings; poor management or favouritism.

questions.question: Outline two ways unresolved conflict between staff can impact a hospitality business.
questions.model_answer: 2+2: impact (1), consequence (1). Model answer: Customer service suffers (1), because guests can sense a tense atmosphere and may not return, harming revenue (1). Staff may resign to escape the conflict (1), forcing the business to spend money recruiting and training replacements (1).

questions.question: List three pathogenic bacteria.
questions.model_answer: "list" means names only, one mark each. Mark scheme: Staphylococcus aureus, Salmonella, E. coli. Any three from the bacteria table earn the marks; spellings close enough to be unambiguous are accepted, but learn them properly.

questions.question: Which bacteria is most associated with cooked rice left at room temperature?
questions.model_answer: Pair each bacteria with its signature food. Rice = B. (Poultry = Salmonella/Campylobacter, soft cheese = Listeria, undercooked mince = E. coli.)

questions.question: State the temperature range known as the danger zone, and name one condition (other than warmth) that bacteria need to multiply.
questions.model_answer: 5°C to 63°C (1); moisture, food or time (1). Number questions are gift marks. Never leave them blank.

questions.question: Explain two ways a food handler can prevent cross- contamination in the kitchen.
questions.model_answer: 2+2. Model answer: Use separate colour-coded boards and knives for raw and cooked foods (1), so bacteria from raw meat cannot transfer onto food that will not be cooked again (1). Store raw meat at the bottom of the fridge (1), so its juices cannot drip onto ready-to- eat food below (1).

questions.question: (new) State how long a food handler must stay away from work after an episode of sickness or diarrhoea, and give one reason why.
questions.model_answer: 48 hours after the symptoms have stopped (1), because the handler can still carry and shed pathogenic bacteria even once they feel completely well (1). The trap is writing "48 hours" alone, or "48 hours after being sick". Say after symptoms stop.

questions.question: (new) Explain what HACCP stands for and describe two things a food business operator must do to run a system based on it.
questions.model_answer: 2+2, with the full name first. Model answer: HACCP stands for Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points (1), a system in which the operator looks at every step from delivery to service and identifies what could make food unsafe (1). The operator must set a measurable limit at each critical point, such as chilling cooked rice within 90 minutes, and record the checks in a log (1). The operator must also train all staff in food hygiene and keep signed, dated training records, because without records the training cannot be proved to an inspector (1).

questions.question: Which food commodity is trussed before cooking?
questions.model_answer: trussing (tying the bird into shape) is a poultry preparation method. Mark scheme answer: poultry. Each preparation verb in the table is a potential MCQ: filleting = fish, de- bearding = mussels, trussing = poultry.

questions.question: State the safe operating temperatures of a deep-freezer and a refrigerator.
questions.model_answer: mark scheme: freezer -18°C (1); fridge 0-5°C (1). Write the minus sign; examiners notice. This exact question opened the sample paper, so treat these two numbers as guaranteed marks.

questions.question: Before cooking, mussels that are open and do not close when tapped should be:
questions.model_answer: Open and unresponsive = dead = dangerous. Answer: B.

questions.question: Explain two reasons why a kitchen should follow product specifications when preparing dishes.
questions.model_answer: 2+2. Model answer: Specifications give consistency (1), because every portion is identical, so returning customers get the dish they expect (1). They control allergens and legality (1), since the dish contains only the listed ingredients and therefore matches the menu description required by law (1).

questions.question: (new) Give one preparation method for each of the following: meat, vegetables, poultry, fish, shellfish.
questions.model_answer: one line per food, one mark each, and stay in preparation (not cooking). Model answer: Meat, mincing (passing meat through a mincer into small strands). Vegetables, blanching (a short plunge in boiling water then iced water). Poultry, trussing (tying the bird into a compact shape with string). Fish, filleting (cutting the flesh from the bone in one piece). Shellfish, de- bearding mussels (pulling off the tough threads and discarding any open shells). The sample paper used exactly this "one per commodity" shape for cooking methods, so expect it for preparation too, and note that the mark scheme rewards a defining phrase.

questions.question: (new) State three rules a chef must follow when storing cooked leftover food in a refrigerator.
questions.model_answer: three separate rules, one mark each, and prefer the ones with numbers in them. Any three from: cool within 90 minutes before refrigerating; use shallow covered containers; label with contents and date; store cooked food above raw food; use within 2-3 days; keep the fridge at 0-5°C; reheat only once to 75°C. Numbers earn marks faster than adjectives.

questions.question: Which dry cooking method uses added oil at 170- 185°C?
questions.model_answer: dry heat plus added fat is roasting's exam fingerprint, and 170-185°C is LRN's roasting range. Mark scheme answer: roasting.

questions.question: Give one cooking method for each of the following, with a definition: meat, vegetables, poultry, fish, shellfish.
questions.model_answer: the definition is half the answer; a method name alone scores half. Mark scheme: meat, braising (cooking in a small amount of liquid); vegetables, steaming; poultry, roasting at 180°C with oil; fish, shallow frying; shellfish, poaching at 75°C. One line per food, method plus a defining phrase.

questions.question: State the safe operating temperature for hot food.
questions.model_answer: mark scheme: over 63°C is safe (1), with 75°C preferable (1). Give both numbers; one number is one mark.

questions.question: Which cooking method uses direct radiant heat and allows fat to drain away?
questions.model_answer: "Radiant heat" and "fat drains" are grilling's exam fingerprints. Answer: C.

questions.question: State the safe core cooking temperature for food, the minimum hot-holding temperature, and the maximum time for cooling hot food before refrigeration.
questions.model_answer: 75°C (1); 63°C (1); within 90 minutes (1). Three numbers, three marks, zero excuses.

questions.question: Describe the difference between roasting and baking.
questions.model_answer: 2+2: both definitions, precisely. Model answer: Roasting cooks food in an oven with hot dry air and added fat, usually at 170-185°C (1), giving meats and vegetables a browned outside and tender inside (1). Baking also uses dry oven heat but without fat added over the food (1), and suits bread, cakes, pastries and potatoes (1).

questions.question: (new) Explain two ways a chef can cool a large pot of hot curry safely before refrigerating it.
questions.model_answer: 2+2, and the "why" is where the second mark lives. Model answer: Divide the curry into smaller, shallow containers (1), because the greater surface area lets heat escape far faster, so the food passes through the danger zone quickly and is cooled within 90 minutes (1). Use a blast chiller, or stand the containers in iced water and stir them (1), which pulls the heat out of the centre and drops the food to below 5°C without warming the fridge and endangering the food already stored there (1).

questions.question: (new) Define poaching and state the approximate temperature at which food is poached.
questions.model_answer: Gently cooking food in liquid held below boiling point, so delicate items such as fish and shellfish keep their shape (1); at around 75°C (1). This is a straight lift from the LRN mark scheme, which gave "shellfish, poaching at 75°C". Whenever a method has a number attached, write the number.

questions.question: Give two examples of each of the following: meat, vegetables, poultry, fish, shellfish.
questions.model_answer: one mark per food group, both examples needed. Mark scheme: meat, beef and lamb; vegetables, carrots and tomatoes; poultry, chicken and turkey; fish, plaice and cod; shellfish, crabs and lobsters. These five commodity lists also feed the preparation and cooking questions in Lesson 10 and Lesson 11; one memorised table pays out three times.

questions.question: Which nutrient found in oily fish supports heart and brain health?
questions.model_answer: Oily fish's exam fingerprint is omega-3. Answer: B.

questions.question: Explain two reasons why a person's diet should include a variety of different food groups.
questions.model_answer: 2+2. Model answer: No single food contains all the nutrients the body needs (1), so variety ensures protein, carbohydrates, fats, vitamins, minerals and fibre are all supplied (1). Variety prevents deficiency diseases (1), for example iron from meat prevents anaemia and vitamin C from vegetables prevents scurvy (1).

questions.question: Describe how (a) canning and (b) freezing affect the nutritional value of vegetables.
questions.model_answer: Two marks each. Model answer: (a) Canning uses high heat (1), which destroys some heat-sensitive vitamins such as vitamin C and some B vitamins, though protein, minerals and fibre survive (1). (b) Freezing keeps most nutrients (1); because vegetables are often frozen quickly after harvest, they can hold more vitamins than "fresh" vegetables stored for days (1).

questions.question: Give one example of each of the following preserved foods: a dried food, a cured food, a vacuum-packed food.
questions.model_answer: One mark each; any correct food scores. Safe picks: dried, raisins or apricots; cured, bacon or corned beef; vacuum-packed, smoked salmon or coffee. Do not give the same food twice under two headings unless it truly fits both (smoked salmon is cured AND often vacuum-packed, but pick different foods to stay safe).

questions.question: Explain why frozen peas can contain more vitamins than "fresh" peas bought from a shop.
questions.model_answer: 2+2. Model answer: Frozen peas are usually frozen within hours of harvest (1), and freezing keeps most nutrients locked in (1). "Fresh" peas may spend days in transport and on shelves (1), and delicate vitamins break down steadily during that storage time (1).

questions.question: Which form of exercise most directly strengthens bones and helps prevent osteoporosis?
questions.model_answer: Bones respond to resistance. Answer: B.

questions.question: Which chemicals, released during exercise, are known as the body's natural "feel-good" chemicals?
questions.model_answer: The mind-benefits list starts with endorphins; it is the exam's favourite single word for this LO. Answer: C.

questions.question: Explain two ways regular exercise can benefit a person's mind.
questions.model_answer: 2+2. Model answer: Exercise releases endorphins (1), the body's natural feel- good chemicals, which reduce stress, anxiety and low mood (1). It improves sleep quality (1), and better rest improves concentration, memory and learning the next day (1).

questions.question: State two impacts of aerobic exercise on the body.
questions.model_answer: Any two: strengthens heart and lungs; improves circulation and stamina; burns calories; lowers blood pressure. "State" needs no explanation; do not waste time writing one.
